Watching this pageant clip, I couldn’t help but ask myself, why do I see what I’ve experienced reflected in almost every interaction between women I come across online?

Not every woman standing beside you is rooting for you. 

Some will smile in your face, applaud your accomplishments, and call themselves your friend, but struggle to genuinely celebrate you when your light starts shining a little brighter than theirs.

And that’s what gets me. 

Why does another woman winning have to feel like you’re losing? 

Why can’t we celebrate each other, open doors for each other, share opportunities, and genuinely want to see each other succeed without comparison, competition, or hidden intentions?

Real sisterhood is more than words. It’s how you show up for women when there’s nothing to gain for yourself. 

It’s celebrating them when they’re in the room and speaking highly of them when they’re not. 

It’s making room at the table instead of trying to knock someone else out of their seat.

Another woman’s crown doesn’t diminish yours. 

Her success doesn’t take away from your own. 

There is room for all of us to grow, shine, and win.

I’ve experienced enough to know that everyone standing beside you isn’t necessarily standing with you. 

Pay attention to who genuinely wants to see you rise and who is waiting for you to fall.

We need more women who understand that supporting another woman doesn’t make you any less. 

It makes room for all of us to win. ❤️

ARIMA uses a time series’s past to forecast what comes next. 📈

Its full name is autoregressive integrated moving average. The three parts work together:
• Integrated: differences between consecutive observations can help create a stationary series.
• Autoregressive: earlier values help predict the next value. After differencing, these are earlier changes.
• Moving average: past forecast errors can shift the next forecast. This is different from averaging recent sales.

In the bakery example, 100, 110 and 118 loaves become changes of 10 and 8. If the next predicted change is 6, the sales forecast becomes 124 loaves.

The settings p, d and q describe the model’s structure. Its numerical weights are learned from historical data, then predictions are checked on later observations.

⚠️ Watch out for:
• Uncertainty further ahead
• Weekly repetition may need SARIMA
• Sudden disruptions to historical patterns

Linear regression, SVM, random forest, XGBoost… which ML algorithm fits which job? 8 essentials side by side 📊

Quick guide to picking a model:
• Predicting a number? Linear regression fits a line by minimizing squared errors.
• Need class probabilities? Logistic regression maps a score into (0, 1).
• Irregular local patterns? K-nearest neighbors votes across the k closest points.
• Clear class gap in high dimensions? SVM maximizes the margin between classes.
• Want readable if-then rules? A decision tree splits features into purer leaves.
• Single tree too noisy? Random forest votes across randomized bootstrap trees.
• Chasing strong tabular accuracy? Gradient boosting (like XGBoost) adds shallow trees to fix remaining errors.
• No labels at all? K-means groups points around K nearest centroids.

Watch how linear, margin, tree, ensemble, and clustering rules carve up data differently.

⚠️ Watch out for:
• Unscaled features in KNN, SVM, and K-means
• Outliers pulling least-squares lines
• Deep trees overfitting without depth or η tuning

The Graduate (1967), directed by Mike Nichols from a screenplay by Buck Henry and Calder Willingham adapted from Charles Webb’s novel, follows Benjamin Braddock (Dustin Hoffman), a recent college graduate returning to his affluent Southern California home. Adrift and alienated, he is seduced by Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft), the wife of his father’s business partner, in an affair that begins as escape and quickly becomes a source of deeper confusion. When he meets and falls for her daughter Elaine (Katharine Ross), Benjamin’s passivity turns into desperate pursuit, culminating in the film’s famous final sequence. The picture captures the restlessness of a young man pressured by parental expectations yet unable to articulate what he wants, set against the polished surfaces of suburban life and scored by Simon & Garfunkel songs that underscore his isolation.

Critically and commercially successful, the film became a defining portrait of generational friction in the late 1960s, blending sharp comedy with an undercurrent of melancholy. Hoffman’s awkward, laconic performance and Bancroft’s poised, predatory Mrs. Robinson created iconic screen figures, while the story’s frank treatment of sex, class, and aimlessness resonated with audiences questioning postwar conformity. Nominated for seven Academy Awards and winning Best Director for Nichols, *The Graduate* influenced subsequent American cinema in its visual style, editing, and willingness to leave its protagonist’s future unresolved. Its closing moments—Benjamin and Elaine on the bus, their expressions shifting from triumph to uncertainty—remain among the most discussed endings in film history, encapsulating the gap between rebellion and the difficulty of knowing what comes next.

😂 GTA players have spent years accusing Los Santos traffic of deliberately swerving into them at the worst possible moment.

Clips like this are exactly why the theory has become such a long-running joke within the GTA community.

One popular explanation claimed Rockstar intentionally used traffic to slow players down at extreme speeds so the game world had more time to load, but former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij recently disputed that theory.

Vermeij explained that the sudden lane changes are random and can become especially abrupt when road-network nodes are positioned too close together.

He did confirm that GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas and GTA IV used certain zones with increased air resistance to limit player speed, just not by intentionally sending NPC cars into their path.

So while GTA traffic can absolutely feel like it has a personal vendetta against you, the chaos appears to be a side effect of how the traffic system behaves rather than a secret anti-speed mechanic.

“You either crashed your A-levels or went to private school.”

That’s what a managing director replied after I emailed his firm looking for an opportunity.

I was a clueless first year sending emails to companies, and I’d clearly caught an executive on a bad day. But once the sting wore off, his reply was the most useful feedback I’d had, because it showed me exactly what I’d got wrong.

• I’d emailed the CFO, whereas the COO was the person who owned hiring for that kind of role.

• I referenced a deal that was six months old, because my outreach system was clumsy, and I now teach clients to find the most up to date information they can.

• Their whole edge was frontier markets and I didn’t mention it once, and relevance is the difference between a reply and getting binned.

• I’d asked for the wrong thing, using a word for a position the firm had never hired for, so now I say contribute or support.

• I’d left my A-levels off my CV, three Bs, and everything you include or leave out still signals something to an employer.

Would I work there now? No. But I’m glad he replied the way he did, because the method he mocked, cold outreach from a nobody, is the one I used to land 15 offers that year.

Rejection is hard to talk about.

But in a season where so many are celebrating med school interviews, residency interviews, acceptances, and exciting news, I know there are also people silently struggling with rejection right now.

I hope this brings you hope.

In college, I applied to an early med program that would’ve let me go to med school without the MCAT or physics: the VERY two things I truly didn’t believe I was capable of.

I never felt like I was strong enough for medicine, so this program felt like my ONE shot - a way in without having to face the doubts I carried so deeply.

Out of thousands of applicants, I was selected for an interview. My hopes skyrocketed. I prepared OBSESSIVELY and gave it everything I had.

And then I was rejected.

I was devastated.

What I couldn’t see then, but understand now, is that this rejection wasn’t a failure. It was a redirection.

That program would’ve taken me far from home and family, far from a life I didn’t yet realize I deeply wanted. I was willing to give up everything to become a doctor, but God knew my heart better than I did.

God was asking me to trust Him - to believe He would walk with me through the uncertainty, and that even closed doors could be part of a plan meant “to prosper and not to harm, to give hope and a future.” Jeremiah 29:11.

Two years later, I ended up exactly where I was meant to be - at the med school I attend now, close to home.

And now I’m applying to residency, once again in a season of interviews, waiting, and trusting God with doors I can’t control.

Funny how life brings you back to the same lessons in different seasons :’)

I share this for three reasons:

1. to be transparent about failure on a platform that too often highlights only the best versions of ourselves

2. to share a piece of my testimony

3. to honor the blessing of a mom who sat with me in the pain and reminded me of God’s truth when I couldn’t see it myself through the tears

maybe someone else needs the reminder today: rejection can be a redirection - one step closer to understanding God’s plan 🤍

✨Crispy Garlic Parmesan Chicken Wrap 🌯

Ingredients

Chicken

* 500g chicken thigh or breast

Marinade

* 1 tsp cayenne powder
* 1 tsp garlic powder
* 1 tsp onion powder
* Salt to taste
* 1 tsp oregano
* 1 tsp dried parsley
* 1/2tsp red chilli flakes
* ½ tsp black pepper
* 1 tbsp ginger & garlic paste
*1tbsp oil

Garlic Parmesan Sauce

* 1 tbsp butter
* 2–3 garlic cloves, minced
* 1 small white onion, finely chopped
* 270ml double cream
* ½ cup whole milk
* 1 tsp cayenne powder
* Salt to taste
* 1 tsp garlic powder
* 1 tsp onion powder
* 1 tsp oregano
* 1 tsp dried parsley
* ½ cup freshly grated Parmesan

Parmesan Fries

* Fries
* Parmesan cheese
* Cayenne powder
* Garlic powder
* Salt to taste

For the Wrap

* Tortilla wraps
* Mozzarella cheese
* Parmesan cheese
* Oil, for frying

Method

Chicken

* Marinate the chicken with all the marinade ingredients for at least 30 minutes.
* Heat 2 tbsp butter and 2 tbsp oil in a pan.
* Cook the chicken over medium heat for 4–5 minutes per side, or until fully cooked. Slice into strips.

Garlic Parmesan Sauce

* Melt the butter with a little oil. Sauté the garlic until lightly golden.
* Add the onion and cook until softened and lightly golden.
* Add the cream and milk, then stir in all the seasonings.
* Cook for 2–3 minutes over medium heat.
* Add the Parmesan and mix until smooth and creamy.

Parmesan Fries

* Toss the fries with Parmesan, cayenne, garlic powder and a little salt.

Assemble

* Spread about 2 tbsp of garlic Parmesan sauce over a tortilla.
* Add Parmesan fries and sliced chicken.
* Top with mozzarella and Parmesan.
* Fold tightly into a wrap.

Crisp the Wrap

* Heat 1–2 tbsp oil in a pan over medium-low heat.
* Cook the wrap for about 2 minutes on each side, until golden and crispy.
* Serve with Parmesan sauce and fries.

Enjoy! 🤍

full recipe with more detailed instructions is linked in my bio on my substack!

🐖 2 lb pork belly, diced ½ inch (try to find a leaner cut)
🍄 8 dried shiitake, soaked (save the liquid)
🧅 6 shallots, thinly sliced + ½ cup oil (or 1 cup store-bought fried shallots)
🧄 4 garlic cloves, minced
🫚 1 inch ginger, minced
🍬 30g rock sugar
🍶 ⅓ cup shaoxing wine
🥢 ¼ cup light soy sauce
🫗 2 tbsp dark soy sauce
🦪 1 tbsp oyster sauce
⭐ 2 star anise
🌰 ½ tsp five spice
🧂 ¼ tsp white pepper
💧 shiitake soaking liquid (1½ cups for instant pot, 2 cups + water for stovetop)
🥚 10 eggs
🥬 1½ lb baby bok choy
🍚 1⅔ cups uncooked jasmine or short-grain rice

1. boil eggs 9 min, ice bath, peel. blanch belly 1 min in the same water, rinse
2. fry shallots in oil until golden, scoop out, keep 1 tbsp oil in the pot
3. render belly 8-10 min, spoon off extra fat, melt rock sugar until amber and toss through
4. add garlic, ginger, shiitake 1 min, deglaze with shaoxing wine and scrape the bottom clean
5. add soy sauces, oyster sauce, spices, fried shallots
6. instant pot: add 1½ cups shiitake liquid, high pressure 25 min, 10 min natural release, then sauté with the eggs 10-15 min until glossy
7. stovetop: add 2 cups shiitake liquid + water to just cover, lowest simmer 60 min, add eggs, simmer 30 min more until the skin is tender
8. blanch bok choy 30-45 sec, ice bath, pat dry
9. pack rice, bok choy, pork + sauce, eggs on the side. keeps 4 days in the fridge

I wish I had some kinda guidance before I started travelling 🤍

I have always really avoided conflict, and so learning how to protect myself and set boundaries travelling - has been a huge journey for me 

It’s so easy to want to diffuse a situation by just excusing it…
“Oh he’s just acting like that because we’re culturally different” 
Or
“he’s not meaning to make me uncomfortable “

For me it was making the decision - I KNOW what I am comfortable with. That does not adjust with my environment.
You do not need to adapt your boundaries for a scenario, or a man’s cultural differences…
If something makes you uncomfortable then it makes you uncomfortable 

Setting boundaries is genuinely a skill and takes practice! Especially when you are young and new to travelling

What I did which really helped, was come up with simple responses - to clearly display my boundaries in any situation.

Having these ready in my head, made knowing what my ‘true self’ would want me to say - much easier, and it prevented me from making excuses for them to avoid conflict in the moment. 

With time it gets easier and less uncomfortable! 

The internet makes it seem like you should go travelling and live like you’re in a movie. This is your reminder that you should be aware always be aware and take precautions, so that you can have the BEST travel experiences possible and gain that worldly knowledge 🥰

DM me If you would like to have an in depth conversation about this - or if setting boundaries is something you struggle with, I can talk with you about what helped me 🤍🥹

caption:
Afraid of not getting into medical school? ☹️⬇️

Follow @journey.with.jayden and I’ll show you how to build an AUTHENTIC application that you can feel confident about.

One thing I was intentional about throughout my premed journey was pursuing experiences that genuinely interested me, NOT just things I thought would impress an admissions committee.

Yes, you need clinical experience, volunteering, leadership, shadowing, and research. Those are the overarching categories to consider.

But what you do WITHIN those categories is where your individuality can shine. 👀

Ask yourself:

➡️ What communities do I want to serve?

➡️ Am I interested in public health, research, business, or something else?

➡️ Are there specific patient populations I’m passionate about, such as children, older adults, or underserved communities?

You don’t have to wait until medical school to start exploring these interests!

And PLEASE don’t feel pressured to have a perfectly crafted “theme” throughout your application.

If you looked at mine, you’d see experiences across several different areas that don’t necessarily fit into one neat box.

YOU ARE NOT ONE-DIMENSIONAL!

You’re more than your GPA, MCAT, clinical hours, or research experiences.

Your application should reflect your passions, interests, personality, and preparation for medicine, not some imaginary version of the perfect applicant.

Build an application that shows admissions committees WHO YOU ARE, not just what you’ve accomplished.

And if you’re struggling to figure out how to do that, my DMs are ALWAYS open! ❤️

I’m here to help you navigate this journey! 🩺

Harvard admitted them. Then Harvard saw the group chat.

In 2017, at least ten admitted students had their Harvard offers taken back after screenshots from a private group chat reached the school. The students thought the chat was private. It wasn’t.

And it isn’t just Harvard. In Kaplan’s 2023 survey, 67% of admissions officers said an applicant’s social media is fair game, and 28% said they have actually gone and looked at a student’s profile. The ones who look say they find something that hurts more often than something that helps.

A private account is not the protection most families think it is. The profile photo, the bio, the tagged pictures, and your student’s comments on other people’s posts are all still visible, and a screenshot can travel anywhere.

Tonight, take two minutes and search your student’s name the way a stranger would. If you can find it, so can they.

CCTV footage from an internet café in Ya'an, Sichuan province, China, has gone viral on social media, drawing widespread praise for the establishment's owner after an accidental equipment collapse. In the video, a cleaning worker finishing her shift in an empty section of the café pushed a gaming chair back toward a long computer desk, inadvertently bumping it and causing the entire row of five desktop computers, monitors, and accessories to crash to the floor.

Visibly shaken by the incident, the worker immediately reported the accident to management and offered to take financial responsibility for the damages, which were estimated at around 10,000 yuan (approximately $1,500). However, instead of demanding compensation, the café owner reviewed the security camera footage and determined that the long desk had not been properly anchored or securely installed.

Refusing to accept any payment from the employee, the owner absorbed the full repair costs himself and thanked the worker for inadvertently exposing a serious structural hazard that could have injured patrons had the seats been occupied. Following the incident, management arranged for technicians to reinforce all computer tables across the venue, earning widespread commendation online for prioritizing workplace fairness and customer safety over financial recovery.

I love my community colleges. I do! BUTTTT… telling a high school senior to skip applying to four-year schools during their senior year? That’s bad advice.

I get the math. Two years free or low-cost at community college, then transfer and pay for two years at a four-year school. That can be a great plan.

But here’s what gets left out. Some scholarships are only for incoming first-year students. So that senior year might be your child’s best shot at a big scholarship from a four-year school. Two years later, they’ll be applying as a transfer student, and the money on the table may look different.

Parents, y’all gotta be careful with that blanket advice. What if the school you crossed off the list would’ve offered your child a full ride? 👀

Apply to BOTH 2- and 4-year this year. See what each school actually offers, compare what you’d pay out of pocket, and let those numbers guide the decision.
